idiom_name: domain interfaces/classes + a mappers module over Prisma/TypeORM/Drizzle data types
implementation_notes: In TypeScript the domain model is a set of interfaces (or classes with private fields and brand types for identifiers and units) in a domain folder, while the data model comes from the persistence tooling - Prisma-generated types, Drizzle row types, or TypeORM entity metadata, which can be kept decorator-free with EntitySchema/separated schema definitions. What replaces the Mapper is a mappers module with pure toDomain/toPersistence functions that also carry validation (often Zod at the boundary); the separation is cheap because types are structural, and that is exactly the risk - a Prisma row and the domain type with the same shape are interchangeable to the compiler, so the mapping layer plus branded primitives are what make the boundary real rather than notional.
pitfalls: Structural typing makes leaks compile clean: a database row can be passed where the domain type is expected, so brands, private fields and mapper-only imports (enforced with lint rules) are the only guard.

Decorator-based entities (TypeORM) require experimentalDecorators/emitDecoratorMetadata and silently put persistence metadata into the class; prefer the separated schema definition when the domain must stay clean.

JSON round-trips and Object.assign/plainToInstance create objects without running constructors or private-field checks, so validation must live in the mapper (Zod or explicit checks) rather than only in the class.
Prisma's generated types are the schema: using them in components couples the UI to the database shape, which is the coupling this pattern exists to break.
